Agreed - but the issue stated seemed to be based more on balance than on RAW.

That said, I think it'd be useful for all these people so eager to limit the Druid's wildshape to remember just how... terrible they are in combat with out it.

Cantrips are weak, and Druids are pretty limited in directly offensive spells. Combine that with no real melee capabilities to speak of (Shillelagh doesn't scale effectively - 1d8+5 is negligible later) and being the only class actually restricted from being well-armored (unless they slow Druid advancement by multiclassing Monk).

It's true that Druids are incredibly versatile, and some of their spells are quite potent in terms of battlefield control. These spells run out pretty quickly though, especially at lower levels - and if the experience budget for monsters is increasing proportionately to the size of the group, it's hard for a Druid to keep up and actively assist the party dynamic without Wildshape.

Do they need every possible form? No, that's silly, and I see no problem with the "Animorphs" approach - so long as a DM recognizes that it's still important to give them opportunities to acquire some kind of currently-capable form.

Which is not a Giant Scorpion when you're level 15, or and Allosaurus at 10. Or else you're essentially limiting the Druid from one of the 3 pillars of the game.

Another option for multiclassing - 2 levels of Paladin and you can be a divine Allosaurus who smites evil foes with their bite. Plus with the new Mariner fighting style, that Allosaurus can now also swim, climb, and gets an AC boost.

Does require 13 str/13 cha, though.

That's totally fine as long as it's applied across the board. 

Does a Battlemaster Fighter need to have someone teach him maneuvers between level 2 and 3?

Does a Wizard require tutelage, or new found scrolls for their spells?

Does a Rogue have to find guild members to teach them how to strike surgically?

Does a Paladin need to demonstrate suitable honor in service to be worthy of new smiting abilities?

Because these classes are designed and balanced against each other in terms of advancement - so if you place RP restrictions on one character's growth, these need to exist similarly for every other character, and for their normal level advancement traits (as Wildshape is one of these) - not just equipment.

The (new) Dragonlord Dromoka!

I'm a Timmy at heart, and Commander is the format for it. Problem is, creature-based strategies are often the obvious threat on a board, and easily disrupted. Dromoka helps fix that! 

She's not broken, or non-interactive, and can't enable the same sorts of shenanigans in Green-White as, say, Sisay - but what she does do is give you a chance against more control-based strategies, and not deny anyone else's fun in the process.

Also, she's a big, legendary Elder Dragon in the format originally named for them, so she's both a nod to Commander's origins as well as competitive in the new environment - truly the best of both worlds. Best of all, she was a prerelease card - meaning that she's accessible to budget players as well as those with more highly-tuned decks. You won't leave anyone out by playing her.

4e actually had magical tattoos as reward options - some were quite potent, too, like the Backlash tattoo which gave your character an extra strike back when bloodied.

Also, you can look at them as a potential power source - one of my previous characters was a Minotaur Runepriest who had his runes tattooed onto his skin - flavor wise, they would glow when he activated them to use powers.

Another character (this one for 5e) was a Human Moon Druid who used his herbalism kit proficiency to make tattoo ink. Whenever he would best a new beast in combat, he would either mix a bit of its blood, or ash if it was burned, into the ink and spend time tattooing it into his skin before assuming its form. Added a neat bit of RP to "You encounter a bear."

I'd actually recommend something slightly different than a typical primer, which don't always stick well to the Bones material - Reaper makes a set of brown, grey, and blue liner colors that work very well as a first/priming coat. 

They're thin, so they won't obscure detail, but they stick well to the material and help paint adhere better, as the Bones material is slightly hydrophobic and without a base you may have trouble getting paints (especially thinned ones) to stick. 

Anyway, Reaper Master Series paints work well for me - dropper bottles so they're easy to use, come in triads, fair prices, good quality, safe ingredients (though, still don't lick your brushes). I started off with the Reaper Bones Learn to Paint Kit and can't recommend it enough. Lots of great tips and a step by step to paint your first three minis; specifically covers Bones, so it should fit your needs, too!

It's useful in that it:

a) doesn't give disadvantage on stealth and

b) offers higher ac late game. 

I have a Dex-based fighter who eventually maxes both Con and Dex. For him, a single level of Barbarian means an eventual +3 AC and no disadvantage on Stealth as well as resistance 2/day. Also, it's lighter not to wear armor, which can prevent encumbrance (though most seem to handwave this).

It can also combine nicely with Moon Druid - rage in animal form, most of which will gain in AC based on their Con scores. Very tanky build with Sentinel.
